title: When Success Creates Its Own Problems
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Notes piece uses the Milwaukee Brewers' 'Timeless Ticket' promotion as a case of unintended consequences. A 2014 offer promised holders the best available seats at any future game, including the World Series, but when the team reached the series in 2026 holders were handed poor seats and no choice of game. The author argues the problem was foreseeable and that great leaders hedge against groupthink and blind spots deliberately. He offers three habits: assign dissent so that someone's job is to break the decision, learn from the people who will be most inconvenienced rather than those closest to the decision, and stress-test a plan against future success as well as failure. The closing line is that a plan or promise that cannot survive success is incomplete.
points: The Brewers' Timeless Ticket promise became a public embarrassment because nobody tested it against the scenario of the team reaching the World Series.
Leaders should assign dissent, making it explicit that the dissenter's job is to break the decision and surface hidden risks.
The most useful feedback comes from those who will be most inconvenienced by a decision, not from those closest to it who are invested in its success.
Leaders in hard times over-weight the consequences of failure and should just as deliberately consider the consequences of success.
Considering unintended consequences should be a routine applied to every decision that matters, not an occasional technique.
quotes: They assign dissent. To deliberately hedge against unintended consequences and groupthink, leaders don’t just invite dissent: They assign it.
They make clear that the dissenter’s job is to break the decision to find hidden impacts, inconsistencies, and risks others have missed.
One mistake leaders often make is to ask the people closest to the decision. But those are often the very people most invested in the decision going well or most afraid to say that it won’t work.
The better move is to seek out those who will be most inconvenienced by the decision or have the least to gain from its succeeding.

When making a tough decision, especially in hard times, many leaders are biased toward considering the consequences of failure. Few take the time to consider, just as deliberately, the consequences of success, no matter how unlikely.
Great leaders make considering unintended consequences an intentional routine, not a technique they occasionally pull off the shelf, and they apply it to every decision that matters.
Most leaders plan for failure, but the best ones also plan for winning. A plan or promise that can’t survive success is always incomplete.
